name: Foot binding

lead: Foot binding was a custom in China in which young girls' feet were broken and tightly wrapped so they stayed small and took on a narrow, arched shape known as the lotus foot. For centuries small bound feet were an ideal of feminine beauty and a signal of status, and they influenced marriage prospects.

It is discussed in appearance culture as a historical example of how beauty standards can reshape bodies. Historians and medical researchers document lasting pain, disability and a higher risk of falls among women who had bound feet.

paras: Historically it began in childhood, usually between about ages four and nine, with long bandages tightened over years. Details of the process are not given here because it is a harmful practice that has ended.

Infection, gangrene and sepsis were common, and some estimates suggest up to 10 percent of girls died. Survivors had chronic pain, difficulty walking and more falls in old age. It was banned in 1912, and the last new cases were reported in 1957.

chain: Conformed to the lotus-foot beauty ideal
angle.text: Binding changed foot shape to meet a prevailing beauty and status ideal. The documented consequences were severe pain and disability, so the wiki records it as history rather than a method.

lead: Foot binding was a Chinese custom in which young girls' feet were broken and tightly wrapped to keep them small. The resulting feet were called lotus feet, and in late imperial China they signalled status and feminine beauty [1]. In appearance culture it is cited as a historical example of a beauty ideal that altered the body, and its harms are well documented.

Accounts trace the custom to the Song dynasty, with possible earliest references around 1100, though court stories linking it to the tenth-century dancer Yao Niang are treated cautiously by historians [1]. It spread from the elite to broader social classes by the Qing era, and by the nineteenth century an estimated 40 to 50 percent of Chinese women had bound feet, with nearly all upper-class Han women [1].

Medical studies of surviving women find lasting effects. A study of women over 70 in Beijing found bound feet in 38 percent of those aged 80 and over and 18 percent of those aged 70 to 79, and these women fell more and had more difficulty squatting and standing from a chair [2].

paras: Zhang Bangji wrote around 1148 that binding was a recent development, and Song-era tombs from 1243 and 1274 contain women with bound feet [1]. Manchu edicts against it in 1636, 1638 and 1664 largely failed [1]. Christian missionaries founded anti-footbinding societies such as the Heavenly Foot Society in Xiamen in 1874, reformers including Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao argued it weakened the nation, and the Republic banned it in 1912 [1]. Rural areas continued into the 1950s, the last new case was reported in 1957 and the last lotus shoe factory closed in 1999 [1].

Interpretations include fashion, status, seclusion, aesthetics and marriage prospects, and scholars such as Dorothy Ko and Patricia Ebrey differ on causes [1]. Some feminist scholars see oppression while others stress mothers' agency and economic reasons [1]. A 2025 review in Clinics in Plastic Surgery uses foot binding as an example of how culture shapes what beauty means [3].

Infection, ingrown nails, necrosis and gangrene were frequent, and survivors had chronic pain and higher risk of falls and fractures [1]. A biomechanical study of historical bound feet found the foot acted as a rigid extension of the lower leg, with the heel bone adapting accordingly [4].

Observational studies of older women with bound feet exist. The Beijing study found they were more likely to fall and less able to squat or rise from a chair [2]. Skeletal studies examine how the heel bone adapted [4].
